chapters.title: Why you're still in it
chapters.teaser: The real reason your soul keeps saying 'let's see where it goes'.

chapters.title: What you actually want
chapters.teaser: Not what sounds chill. What you'd ask for if you weren't worried.

chapters.title: How you read mixed signals
chapters.teaser: Your decoding habit, and a better way to get information.

chapters.title: The talk, your way
chapters.teaser: How to ask 'what are we' in words that fit your soul.

chapters.title: Your line
chapters.teaser: The one thing you shouldn't keep accepting.

chapters.title: Either way, you're okay
chapters.teaser: What comes next, whatever answer you get.

text.why-you-stay: Gap Wood doesn't quit things. You see potential, you see a direction, and you'd rather build than walk away. In a situationship that instinct can keep you planting in soil that never agreed to be a garden. You tell yourself it's growing slowly, that they need time, that you'll know more next month. Sometimes that's true. Often you're staying because leaving would feel like admitting a project failed. Ask yourself plainly: am I here because this feels good now, or because I've already invested so much? Those are very different reasons, and only one of them is about joy.
text.what-you-want: You probably know exactly what you want. You just haven't said it, because for Gap Wood saying it out loud means committing to the outcome. Try anyway, privately first. Write one sentence that starts with I want a relationship where, and finish it honestly. Exclusive? Plans beyond next weekend? Being introduced to their friends? Tall trees like clarity. Not knowing where something is heading is genuinely uncomfortable for you, and that discomfort is information. It's telling you that casual may not be what you signed up for, even if you said it was at the start.
text.mixed-signals: When signals are mixed, you tend to grab the most hopeful one and build a plan on top of it. A good date becomes evidence of a shared future. Gap Wood reads intention into action and assumes other people move as purposefully as you do. Many don't. A warm night may simply mean they had a warm night. The fix isn't becoming cynical. It's to stop interpreting and start asking. You're good at direct questions in every other part of your life, at work, with family, with friends. You can be good at them here too.
text.the-talk: Done your way, the talk should be simple, calm, and early in the evening, not after drinks. Gap Wood is persuasive, so the risk is turning it into a pitch for why you two should be together. Don't sell. State. Something like: I like you, and I'm looking for something more defined. What are you looking for? Then stop talking. Truly stop. Let their answer be their answer, without arguing with it or offering a revised proposal. You're not negotiating a contract. You're finding out where another person stands, which is a different and much shorter conversation.
text.your-line: Your line is direction. Gap Wood can tolerate slow, but not nowhere. Decide now what you won't keep accepting: maybe being someone's secret, or plans that always shift at the last minute, or months with no definition at all. Write it down and keep it somewhere you'll see it. When you reach that line, you don't need a dramatic exit, only a calm, clear sentence: this isn't working for me. Respecting your line isn't a threat or an ultimatum. It's self-respect, and it's the same quality that makes people trust you everywhere else.
text.either-way: Yes or no, you'll be okay, and you'll know more than you know now. If they want more, wonderful, build it slowly and together. If they don't, you've saved yourself months of growing toward a wall. Gap Wood recovers by redirecting energy, so give yourself a short, real pause first, then put that drive into something that grows back: a goal, a friendship, a fresh start. Clarity costs one slightly awkward conversation. Uncertainty costs a great deal more, paid out slowly in checked phones and second-guessed evenings. You're far better at new beginnings than you give yourself credit for.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: You see so much potential in them, Gap. That's lovely.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Potential isn't a relationship. It's a pitch deck.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: It's okay to want something defined.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Then define it. You plan everything else down to the minute.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Ask, then really listen to the answer.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: No selling. No rebuttals. Ask once. Listen once.

spring.intro: Spring Gap Wood wants to know where things are growing, and fast. Wood commanded your birth season, doubling your own element, so you like direction, labels and a plan you can stand behind. A situationship should drive you up the wall, and secretly it does. So why are you still in one? Often because you decided to be the patient one, the bigger tree, the person who doesn't need to ask. Pride dressed up as chill. The spring tree's honest move is the one it's best at: stand up straight and say what you want. You're not built for vague. You never were. Stop pretending the fog suits you.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: You, the most decisive tree alive, have been seeing where it goes since March?

summer.intro: A summer tree burns its energy outward, and Fire ruled the month you were born, Gap. Wood feeds Fire, so you express care loudly: plans, favors, enthusiasm, the effort of three people. In a situationship that means you're probably doing most of the work. You suggest the dates, keep the chat alive, show up with snacks. And because you're giving, it feels like a relationship to you, while it may feel like a nice warm hobby to them. Summer Gap's lesson is to notice the ratio. Stop fueling it for a week and watch what they put in. Their effort, not your fire, tells you what this is.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Try pausing the effort for a week. Let them show you their half.

autumn.intro: Autumn put Metal in charge of your birth season, Gap, and Metal is the axe to your tree. You grew up with rules and a quiet dread of being cut down. In a situationship that can make you careful in a way that doesn't look like you. You hold back the question because asking feels like handing someone the axe. So you wait, prune your own needs and call it being low-maintenance. Here's the autumn twist: Metal also shapes Wood into something useful. A clear boundary is your best tool, not your enemy. Decide your own terms first. Then a no from them is information, not a verdict.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Calling yourself low-maintenance while quietly starving is not a personality, Gap.

winter.intro: Winter Gap Wood lives on what's underground. Water ruled your season and Water nourishes Wood, so you can survive a long time on very little sunlight: a good text here, a memorable night there. That's exactly how a situationship keeps you. You're rooted enough to wait and patient enough to make it look fine. But being able to live on scraps isn't the same as being fed. The winter blind spot is mistaking endurance for contentment. Ask yourself what you'd want if spring arrived tomorrow. If the answer is more than this, you already know. Waiting quietly won't make them guess it.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: You can survive on crumbs, Gap. You deserve a whole meal.

earth.intro: The Earth days end every season, Gap, and you were born in them: a tall tree in heavy ground. Wood controls Earth, so you treat a situationship like terrain to manage. You map it, plan around it, and keep it moving forward in your head while saying very little out loud. The other person may think you're casual. You're actually building. The drift happens because your plans are silent. The talk for you is short and structural: what you want, what you're offering, and a clear question. Then let them answer without managing the reply.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: You've drawn up blueprints, Gap. They haven't seen a single page.

strength.strong: Your chart backs your tree with plenty of Wood and Water, Gap, so you're sure of yourself and slow to bend. In a situationship that confidence can look like control. You might decide when you meet, what you do and how fast things move, then wonder why they stay noncommittal. Or you push for a label like it's a negotiation you plan to win. The blind spot of a strong tree is crowding the other plant. Give them room to step toward you. Ask what they want, then actually listen. Commitment chosen freely lasts longer than commitment won.
strength.weak: With little support around your Day Master, Gap, you stand tall by effort. In a situationship you might accept less than you'd tolerate anywhere else: late replies, last-minute plans, a label that never arrives. You tell yourself you're being easygoing. It's closer to shrinking. A tree that doubts its roots bends toward any light. Your needs aren't excessive. Write down three things you'd want from a relationship, then compare them with what you're getting. If the gap is wide, you deserve to say so, calmly and once.

balance_text.too_much_wood: Too much Wood means you push for growth and definition. In a situationship you might rush clarity, or picture a whole future before the other person has caught up to the present. Your drive is a good thing. Just give them room to answer at their own pace once you've asked. Ask once, clearly, then step back and let the answer come. Balance with a little Metal: clear boundaries, finished business, knowing when something needs pruning rather than more growth.
balance_text.missing_wood: Missing Wood means starting things, including the talk, feels hard. You might let an undefined situation drift on and on simply because initiating anything feels heavy. Build momentum in small steps: decide what you want, write it down, choose a day to ask. Spend time outdoors and around green things. You don't need to grow everything at once. You only need one honest question, asked once, out loud.
balance_text.too_much_fire: Too much Fire means big feelings, fast. In a situationship you might swing between excitement and frustration in the same evening, and want answers right now. Slow your pace a little. Pick a calm moment for the talk, not a heated one. Cool down with water: rest, quiet nights in, a walk before sending any big message. Your passion is attractive. Just don't let it make your decisions at midnight.
balance_text.missing_fire: Missing Fire means expressing feelings and being seen can feel hard. You might keep this situationship low-key so that nobody, including you, has to admit it matters. Turn the light up a little. Let your feelings show in small ways. Be visible in your own life too: plans, friends, sunlight, music. The more you shine for yourself, the easier the honest question becomes when you finally ask it.
balance_text.too_much_earth: Too much Earth means you wait, stay steady, and stay put, sometimes for too long. In a situationship you may tolerate a lack of definition because change feels disruptive and messy. Bring in a bit of movement: pick a day by which you'll have the talk, and keep it. Let some Wood in, growth and fresh starts. Stable doesn't have to mean stuck, and patient doesn't have to mean silent.
balance_text.missing_earth: Missing Earth means stability is hard to find, and an undefined relationship can make you feel even more unsteady than usual. Ground yourself first: routines, regular meals, a dependable circle of friends. Then have the talk from a steady place, not a shaky one. You'll think more clearly and ask more clearly when your own ground is solid under your feet, whatever the answer turns out to be.
balance_text.too_much_metal: Too much Metal means you want clarity and might cut too fast to get it. In a situationship you may issue ultimatums or go cold the moment things feel vague. Your boundaries are strong, which is good. Soften the delivery: ask with curiosity first, decide second. Water helps here: rest, reflection, letting a feeling be felt before you act on it.
balance_text.missing_metal: Missing Metal means boundaries are hard. In a situationship you may accept less than you want and keep telling yourself it's fine. Practice clear edges: decide your line and write it down somewhere you'll see it. Say no to plans that don't work for you. White and silver, decluttering, finishing things all support you. A boundary isn't harsh. It's honesty about what you need.
balance_text.too_much_water: Too much Water means overthinking and very deep feeling. In a situationship you might analyze every message and drown in what-ifs that never happen. Your intuition is valuable, but it needs a shore to land on. Earth helps: routines, physical activity, friends who ground you. Put a limit on the analysis. Ask the question instead of guessing the answer.
balance_text.missing_water: Missing Water means reflection and rest get skipped. You might keep the situationship busy and fun so you never have to stop and think about what it actually is. Make space for quiet: a journal, a slow evening, a moment alone to ask yourself what you really want here. Clarity starts inside you before it's ever spoken to them, and it's worth the quiet.

too_much_wood.speaker: yeon
too_much_wood.text: Too much Wood: you've planned your future together. They haven't planned Saturday.

too_much_wood.speaker: bom
too_much_wood.text: That growing energy is lovely. Point it at what you want, not only at them.

too_much_fire.speaker: yeon
too_much_fire.text: Too much Fire: one great date and you're naming the dog. Breathe.

too_much_fire.speaker: bom
too_much_fire.text: Your passion is magnetic. Let them match it before you double it.

too_much_earth.speaker: yeon
too_much_earth.text: Heavy Earth: you've waited so patiently you've basically become their furniture.

too_much_earth.speaker: bom
too_much_earth.text: Your steadiness is a gift. It's fair to ask for steadiness back.

too_much_metal.speaker: yeon
too_much_metal.text: Lots of Metal: you've drafted an ultimatum. Maybe try a question first.

too_much_metal.speaker: bom
too_much_metal.text: Your clarity is strength. Soften the delivery and it lands beautifully.

too_much_water.speaker: yeon
too_much_water.text: Overflowing Water: you analyzed one 'haha' with three friends and a tarot app.

too_much_water.speaker: bom
too_much_water.text: Your sensitivity notices so much. Check the signals against actual actions too.

missing_wood.speaker: bom
missing_wood.text: Missing Wood can make it hard to picture what you want. Try imagining it.

missing_wood.speaker: yeon
missing_wood.text: No Wood, no vision. You're seeing where it goes without looking anywhere.

missing_fire.speaker: bom
missing_fire.text: Missing Fire can make it hard to show interest. A little warmth helps.

missing_fire.speaker: yeon
missing_fire.text: No Fire. They genuinely cannot tell if you like them. Neither can I.

missing_earth.speaker: bom
missing_earth.text: Missing Earth makes it easy to drift. Choose one thing you're sure about.

missing_earth.speaker: yeon
missing_earth.text: No Earth, no ground. You change your mind about them every other day.

missing_metal.speaker: bom
missing_metal.text: Missing Metal can blur your line. You can decide what you won't accept.

missing_metal.speaker: yeon
missing_metal.text: No Metal means no line. You'll accept 'wyd' at midnight forever.

missing_water.speaker: bom
missing_water.text: Missing Water can make feelings hard to say. Try writing them first.

missing_water.speaker: yeon
missing_water.text: No Water. You'd rather move countries than say 'I like you.'

gap-wood.title: Two trees, one unasked question
gap-wood.text: Two Gap Woods in a situationship is a strange thing to watch. You can plan a weekend away down to the train platform, split a spreadsheet for groceries, argue about the best route up a hill, and still not have said one word about what this is. Each of you is waiting for the other to ask, because asking first feels like losing a point. So the drift is not vague at all on the surface. It is very organized. It just has no name. You both watch each other's Instagram stories within minutes and neither of you replies to them, which is its own little standoff. The signal you send is competence: look how fine I am. The signal coming back is the same, and you both read it as indifference. The talk for this pair works best when it is not a negotiation. No agenda, no opening position. Try something almost too simple: I like you, and I'd like us to be a real thing. I'm not trying to win this one. Being the first tree to bend is not weakness here. It is the only move that gets you out of a very polite stalemate.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: You two planned the train times but not the relationship. Adorable, honestly.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Someone has to ask first. Pride is not a love language.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Bending once won't make you any shorter, Gap.

eul-wood.title: The tree, the vine and the maybe
eul-wood.text: With an Eul Wood, the situationship tends to grow sideways while you stand still. Eul is warm in a hundred small ways: voice notes on the walk to work, a link to a flat in Lisbon neither of you can afford, a sticker of a cat looking judgmental. It feels like a relationship. Then you ask a straight question about the weekend and get a cheerful answer that somehow isn't one. You call that dodging. Eul would probably call it keeping things light. Your signal, from Eul's side, is the one-word reply. You type 'ok' meaning yes, sounds good, and it lands like a closed door. Eul's signal is breadth: lots of contact, very little commitment language. Neither signal is the whole truth. For the talk, don't bring a conclusion. Gap Wood tends to arrive with the verdict already written. Bring a question and one warm sentence: I love how much we talk. I'm also starting to want this to be clear. Where are you with it? Let Eul answer in Eul's own roundabout way, and ask a second time, gently, if the first answer wanders. Your job is to be honest without becoming the wall Eul has to climb around.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Eul's voice notes and Gap's 'ok' are both affection. Different dialects.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: One of you needs to stop wriggling. The other needs more than one word.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Clear question first, cat sticker second.

byeong-fire.title: Firewood for a sun that forgets to look down
byeong-fire.text: Byeong Fire is the most fun part of your week, and you know it. The spontaneous Thursday drinks, the photo of a stranger's dog sent with eleven exclamation marks, the way a room gets louder when Byeong walks in. You, meanwhile, are quietly supplying the firewood: the lifts home, the listening, the planning that makes the spontaneous things actually happen. Byeong doesn't mean to take it for granted. A sun just doesn't look down much. The drift here is uneven giving. You keep a mental ledger without meaning to, and the day Byeong goes silent after a big night, you start counting hours. Then Byeong floods back with voice notes as if nothing happened, because from Byeong's side nothing did. Your signal is reliability, and it can look like you're fine with exactly this. For the talk, skip the principle. You love a principle, and Byeong hears a principle as a lecture. Keep it warm and personal: I love being around you. I'm giving a lot to this, and I'd like to know if we're building something. How do you see us? If you notice you've rehearsed it like a presentation, cut it in half.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Byeong forgets to say thank you out loud. The logs don't chop themselves.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Gap, stop counting the silent hours and just say what you need.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Warm talk, short talk. No slides.

jeong-fire.title: The timetable and the 1 a.m. paragraph
jeong-fire.text: With a Jeong Fire, the situationship can feel calm on your side and quietly intense on theirs. You text like a train timetable: arriving 7, still on for Friday, good. Jeong writes at 1 a.m., a careful paragraph about a song that reminded them of you, and then notices that your reply was four words. You didn't mean anything by it. Jeong may still have read something into it. The drift in this pair is invisible. You assume silence means all is well, because for you it does. Jeong tends to hold small hurts in, let them flicker, and test the water instead of saying the thing. So the question of what you are can sit unspoken for weeks, while you think it's going great and Jeong is wondering if you even noticed there was a question. Your strongest signal is that you keep turning up. Make it visible: reply to the 1 a.m. paragraph with one detail that proves you read it. When you have the talk, don't try to fix anything. Just ask: I really like what we have. What do you want it to be? Then let Jeong take their time. A candle needs still air.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Jeong's 1 a.m. paragraphs are lovely. Gap reads them like weather reports.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Gap doesn't do subtext. Hinting at a tree is a hobby, not a plan.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Gap, send one detail back. That's all the candle needs.

mu-earth.title: Pushing a mountain to see if it's interested
mu-earth.text: A situationship with a Mu Earth can feel like pushing a mountain to see if it's interested. You suggest the weekend trip, the new restaurant, the dinner with your friends. Mu says 'maybe', and then nothing, and then a reply four hours later that is perfectly sincere and doesn't move anything forward. You start to read stillness as rejection. Mu probably reads your pushing as pressure. The drift here isn't vague plans so much as unmoving ones. Mu tends to like what is, and a situationship can be very comfortable for a mountain: same café, same Sunday, no big conversations. You want growth. You also have a habit, worth owning, of quietly improving the people you date. Suggesting a better job, a better gym, a better sofa. Mu feels that as roots cracking rock. For the talk, lower the pressure and raise the clarity. Don't pitch a future. Ask one thing: I'd like us to be official. Is that something you want, or do you like it as it is? Give Mu room to answer, and agree that slow is not the same as no. If you can't live with the answer, that is information too.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Mu's four-hour reply is sincere. It just arrives on mountain time.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Gap, stop renovating the mountain. It wasn't for sale.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Mu needs to say it out loud once. Silence isn't a sentence.

gi-earth.title: Comfortable enough to skip the label
gi-earth.text: The pull between you and a Gi Earth is gentle and real. 甲 and 己 are one of the classic combinations, the tree that finds its garden, and you've probably felt it: you relax around Gi in a way you don't around most people. That ease is exactly why this situationship can drift. It's so comfortable that it doesn't seem to need a name. Gi sends the check-ins: did you eat, how did the presentation go, home safe? You reply with news. It works, until you notice you haven't asked a single thing back in a week. Gi tends to absorb rather than object. If Gi wants more clarity, Gi may not say it. Gi may just worry about it privately, while helping you pick a birthday present for your mom. The signal from Gi is care. The signal from you can look like you're receiving it as a service. For the talk, start by asking, not telling: How are you feeling about us, honestly? Listen to the whole answer, including the careful part at the end. Gi often keeps the important thing for last. Say what you want, too. Just say it after you've asked.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: 甲己 is a lovely pull. Comfort is not the same as clarity, though.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Gi knows the coffee order and still doesn't know where things stand.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Gap, ask how Gi is. Really ask.

gyeong-metal.title: Radio chatter and a dishwasher war
gyeong-metal.text: A Gyeong Metal is honest with you in a way that's thrilling at first. No games, no vague maybes, no 'haha we'll see'. Your texts look like a military radio: 'Friday?' 'Yes.' 'Where.' 'Mine.' It's efficient and a little bit hot. The drift starts when the honesty turns into notes. Gyeong criticizes to improve things, and somewhere between your shoes and your opinion on a film, you start to feel graded. You defend your position. Gyeong pushes. Two people who agree on most of life end up arguing about the correct way to load a dishwasher in a flat neither of you shares. In that heat, the bigger question of what you are gets parked, because neither wants to look soft. Your signal to Gyeong is principle, and when it comes as a speech it lands as a sermon. For the talk, no lecture, no closing argument. Gyeong respects short and true: I want this to be serious. Do you? Then stop talking. If the conversation sharpens, add one soft line on purpose. It costs you nothing and it changes the whole temperature of steel.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: You two agree on almost everything. Except who is right.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Gyeong treats the dishwasher like a referendum. The axe can go down.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Gap, no sermon. One true sentence.

sin-metal.title: A paragraph answered with a thumbs up
sin-metal.text: A Sin Metal notices everything. The new jacket, the typo in your text, the fact that you said 'we'll see' about their friend's birthday dinner. Sin picks gifts that make you feel understood and sends texts that were clearly reread before sending. And you reply 'ok 👍'. To you, that's a full sentence. To Sin, it's a small cold draft. The drift here is appreciation leaking away. Sin puts effort into the details of this thing and wants it seen. You assume effort is normal and don't comment. Meanwhile Sin's precise little remarks, about your timing, your manners at their friend's dinner, the way you told a story too loudly, start to feel like a quality review. So you go a bit blunt and Sin goes a bit polished, and the question of what you are hangs there, neatly unanswered. Your signal is matter-of-fact, which reads as unbothered. For the talk, open with something specific you value. Not 'you're great'. Something like: I love that you remembered my sister's name. Then the real thing: I want to be with you properly. Do you? And then, crucially, don't shrug at the answer.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Sin's carefully chosen words deserve better than a thumbs up.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Gap, 'ok 👍' is not a reply to a paragraph. Try a compliment.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Sin's hints bounce off trees. Plain words work better.

im-water.title: The calendar invite and the riverbank
im-water.text: Im Water feeds you. The conversations go deep, the ideas get bigger, and you've never had someone talk about the future of cities with you at 2 a.m. and make it sound romantic. Then Im disappears for a day and resurfaces with three paragraphs about a documentary. You want to be pleased about the three paragraphs. You mostly want to know where the day went. The drift between you has a name, and naming it helps: when Im feels fenced in, Im goes vague; when you feel unsure, you tighten the plan. So you send a calendar invite, Im sends a 'let's see how the week goes', and both of you feel a little misunderstood. Your signal, from Im's side, can look like a dam being built. Im's signal, from yours, looks like a river that won't commit to a riverbed. For the talk, don't open with structure. Open with what Im gives you, then say what you need: I want us to be together. I don't need to know where you are every hour. I do need to know we're a thing. Agree on a small anchor, like one check-in a day, and leave the rest of the water free.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Im's midnight essays are gorgeous. A two-word check-in matters too.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Gap, a calendar invite is not a love letter.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Name the loop and it loses half its grip.

gye-water.title: The moon screenshot and 'thursday 7?'
gye-water.text: Gye Water is the kind of person who sends you a screenshot of the moon with no caption, and you're never quite sure if it's a love letter or just a moon. With you, Gye is gentle rain: they notice when you're tired, they remember the thing you mentioned once, they make the hard week softer. Your answer to the moon is usually 'nice, are we still on for Thursday?' The drift here is that Gye hints and you schedule. Gye keeps feelings close and lets them out sideways, in songs and half-finished thoughts. You're direct, and when you want answers you push, and pushing tends to make Gye go misty. So you ask what this is, Gye says something lovely and vague, and you leave the conversation with less information than you started with. Your signal is certainty, which can feel like pressure to someone who processes slowly. For the talk, answer the feeling first. If Gye sends a song, say what it made you feel before asking anything. Then ask softly and give space: I'd love for us to be official. No rush to answer tonight. With Gye, mist is often thinking, not evasion.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Gye's moon screenshot is beautiful. It needs a sentence under it.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Gap, 'nice, thursday 7?' is not how you answer the moon.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Answer the feeling first, then the logistics.
